newsitem.title: USA: U.S. governors applaud budget deal,childrens' health.
newsitem.headline: U.S. governors applaud budget deal,childrens' health.

text.p: State governors attending their annual meeting Tuesday hailed the budget agreement between President Clinton and House Republicans, especially provisions to extend health care to poor children.

"In charting a new course toward expanding (medical insurance) coverage to more uninsured children, Congress and the president are giving states the ability to build on their successes in designing health insurance programmes that meet the unique needs of their states," they said in a joint statement.
The 50 governors applauded the president and Congress for giving states the opportunity to continue what they termed their success in extending care to more uninsured children.

"Governors have made significant progress in extending coverage to uninsured children," said the National Governors' Conference Chairman Gov. Bob Miller of Nevada and vice chairman, Ohio's George Voinovich.
"With state flexibility to design more meaningful and comprehensive benefits packages, coverage numbers will increase substantially," the governors said.

A five-year balanced budget deal worked out between Clinton and the White House includes $24 billion over five years in grants that states could use to expand health care to many of the nation's 10 million uninsured children.

The children's health programme is one of the most ambitious initiatives in the budget. Republican leaders initially resisted children's care efforts, which congressional Democrats declared early this year as their No. 1 health priority.

The White House had wanted uniform health benefits, including prescription drugs, vision, hearing and mental health. Republican lawmakers and governors wanted to give states maximum flexibility to design their own programmes.
The compromise lets governors choose from three insurance options, including their largest health maintenance organisation or a state employee benefit plan.
States would not have to provide the actual insurance policy, but could offer their own programme if it was the "actuarial" or dollar value equivalent.

Governors could also use the funds to expand existing Medicaid programmes for the poor and would have to put up some of their own money to get the grants. The federal funds could be used to provide care to children in families with incomes up to 200 percent of poverty, or $32,100 for a family of four.
Children's advocates hailed the deal as an important step, but warned the legislation did not guarantee uniform benefits.

"There will be political fights in state capitols over which benefits children get, the challenge will be to keep children's health insurance first rather than special interests," said Stan Dorn of the Childrens' Defence Fund.

The governors, meeting in Las Vegas for their annual conference, noted that 40 states have expanded Medicaid coverage beyond federally mandated levels and said the governors were looking forward to working with Congress and the White House to expand health care access to even more children.
